newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. airman in Okinawa quizzed over alleged rape.
newsitem.headline: U.S. airman in Okinawa quizzed over alleged rape.

text.p: A U.S. airman stationed at Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, southern Japan, is being questioned over a complaint by a Japanese woman that she was raped in the base compound, U.S. air force officials said on Wednesday.
"The case is still under investigation under the provisions of Article 32 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice," a spokesman at the base told Reuters.

A hearing on Thursday will determine whether the allegation should be referred to a court martial or if some other form of action should be taken, according to a statement released late on Tuesday by the base's public affairs office.
The incident allegedly occurred on the evening of August 10, and the woman, who reported it to base authorities, asked that further details not be revealed, the spokesman said.

Earlier this year, three U.S. servicemen were jailed for abducting and raping an Okinawan girl in September 1995. That case led to a tremendous public outcry against the concentration of U.S. bases in Okinawa.
The island prefecture constitutes less than one percent of Japan's total land area, but about one-fifth of the island is taken up by U.S. military facilities.

The subtropical island, some 1,000 km (625 miles) southwest of Tokyo, is home to three-quarters of the U.S. military facilities in Japan and about half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel stationed in the country.
The issue of the huge concentration of U.S. military facilities on Okinawa has complicated U.S-Japan security ties.

In New York on Tuesday, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, visiting the United States to attend the U.N. General Assembly, met U.S. President Bill Clinton and in their meeting referred to the bases issue.
The two leaders stressed their mutual commitment to addressing grievances on Okinawa about the heavy concentration of U.S. military bases there.
Following the 1995 rape case, Okinawa's governor, Masahide Ota, had refused to sign orders for renewal of land lease contracts for U.S. military facilities.
The leases, held by some 3,000 landowners opposed to the bases, expire next May, posing a potential threat to U.S. use of the facilities.
In a referendum earlier this month, Okinawans voted overwhelmingly in favour of shrinking the U.S. military presence, resented for the noise, accidents and crime by U.S. troops.

But Ota relented and agreed to sign the order earlier this month after Hashimoto pledged to shrink the bases and set up a five billion yen ($45.5 million) fund for the economic development of Okinawa Prefecture.
